entry.dc:title: Evaluation of runoff and erosion from surface-mined areas.
entry.dc:creator: Hartley D.
entry.dc:description: The purpose of this chapter is to present and discuss methods of calculating runoff and soil loss from surface mined areas. The section will be of primary interest to the surface mine hydrologist because applications stress typical surface mine problems. However, the methods included herein are not exclusively surface mine methods and should be of interest to engineers, planners and concerned citizens who wish to evaluate the response of watersheds to agricultural, construction, or other disturbances. One of the most difficult tasks facing the surface mine hydrologist is to determine the probable hydrologic consequences (PHC) of planned mining activities. The effect of these activities on surface runoff and sediment yield need to be evaluated for both PHC determination and for design of impact mitigation measures such as sediment ponds, diversion channels, culverts and surface treatments. Consequently, this chapter focuses on predictive methods which quantitatively estimate the surface runoff and erosion response to anticipated landscape disturbances caused by mining. (from paper)

entry.dc:title: Iron and manganese removal within a wetland constructed for the treatment of acid mine drainage. M.Sc. thesis
entry.dc:creator: Stillings L.
entry.dc:description: As an alternative to chemical treatment of mine drainage, a Typha-dominated wetland was constructed on a seep draining a reclaimed surface mine in Tuscarawas County, Ohio. The wetland substrate consisted of a basal limestone layer and an upper layer of humic soil. Typha (cattails) were transplanted into the basin from surrounding areas. A hydrologic budget, consisting of surface flow, precipitation, and evaporation components, demonstrated that surface flow from the seep contributed approximately 97% of the water which entered, and exited, the basin. Mass budgets, created from hydrologic and chemical data, revealed that 67% of the 186 kg of iron introduced to the system during the sample period was removed from the waterflow. Manganese removal was less successful. Periods of increased waterflows corresponded with the smallest percent reduction of influent mass concentrations. Basin length and substrate throughflow affected iron and manganese removal. -from Author

entry.dc:title: Evaluating the effect of rock parameters on surface mine blasting by finite element analysis
entry.dc:creator: Sunu M.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: The blasting process in surface mines involves extremely complex interactions. Utilizing Finite Element (FE) analysis, the effect of rock mass properties and discontinuity data can be fairly idealized and assessed. The purpose of this paper is to present the application of finite element methods to fragmentation due to blasting in surface mining operations. As a result, the prediction and extent of blasting will help the engineers engaged in surface mining and construction operations to use explosives efficiently. © 1988, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Pneumoconiosis in iron ore surface mining in labrador
entry.dc:creator: Martin J.R.
entry.dc:description: A cross-sectional survey of the work force at an iron ore surface mine and beneficiation plant in Labrador identified cases with a radiologic diagnosis compatible with simple pneumoconiosis by the International Labour Organization (ILO) classification (1980). Their distribution by ILO categories 1, 8, and 3, after excluding those with confounding diagnoses for pneumoconiosis, was 30, 10, and 2 cases, respectively. ILO category was related to age, duration of current employment, andcumulative respirable dust and quartz levels, as well as to decrement in ventilatory function. © by American Occupational Medical Association.

entry.dc:title: Petrographic zonation within the Waynesburg coal
entry.dc:creator: Renton J.
entry.dc:description: The Waynesburg coal was sampled with four columns of oriented blocks; three columns within one surface mine and a fourth from a surface mine approximately 1.6 km distant. Each column was described as to lithotype based upon the relative abundance of bright and dull banding. Each lithotype band was sampled and analyzed for maceral and mineral matter content which was in turn used to delineate petrographic zones within the coal. Statistical analysis of the data showed that the two benches of the coeal were different in maceral composition but similar in the amount of mineral matter they contained. The petrographic data showed that laterally persistent zones of petrographic similarity are recognizable within the study area which reflect the geochemical and depositional history of the original peat-forming swamp. © 1988.

entry.dc:title: Mine drainage and surface mine reclamation conference, Pittsburgh, April 1988. Abstracts and program
entry.dc:creator: Plass W.T.
entry.dc:description: The ca.140 abstracts are arranged in the 20 session themes. These basically cover: acid mine drainage (prediction, field applications, general); mine hydrology; revegetation research; post-mining land use; wetland and wildlife habitat restoration; growth media and amendments; natural reclamation processes; wetland systems for mine water treatment (case studies, process and design); reclamation with trees, abandoned mine lands (ground control, fire control); biological mine water treatment; policy issues; mine geochemistry, successful bond release practices; mine waste characterization. -M.A.Bass

entry.dc:title: Municipal sludge for minespoil reclamation: I. Effects on microbial populations and activity
entry.dc:creator: Seaker E.
entry.dc:description: A field study of five coal surface mine sites reclaimed with sewage sludge and one site reclaimed by conventional methods (chemical fertilizer) was conducted to assess the effects of sludge amendments and time on populations of bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes, and on microbial respiration and organic matter decomposition. The sludge-amended sites ranged in age from 1 to 5 yr following sludge application at rates of 120 to 134 Mg ha<sup>-1</sup> (dry wt. basis). All sites were planted to grass and legume cover. Populations of aerobic heterotrophic bacteria, fungi, and Nitrobacter, and soil respiration rate, were highest on the 1-yr-old site due to the high organic matter input. On the four older sites, values decreased, but remained within the ranges reported for undisturbed soils. Acintomycete populations peaked on the 3- and 4-yr-old sites, while populations of Nitrosomonas were not related to the age of the site. Decomposition rate was lowest on the 1-yr-old site, and increased significantly with site age. As measured by microbial populations and activity, ecosystem recovery on the sludge-amended sites appeared to be occurring at a more rapid rate than on the fertilizer-amended site, which after 5 yr, exhibited sparse microbial populations and low activity. The microbial populations in the sludge-amended spoil were not adversely affected by the heavy metals applied in the sludge, when compared with populations of soil microbes reported for undisturbed soils.

entry.dc:title: Phosphorus and potassium relationships in southwestern Virginia coal-mine spoils
entry.dc:creator: Howard J.
entry.dc:description: The paper reports on a study into the P and K relationships of representative mine spoils and contiguous natural soils derived from the Wise Formation in southwestern Virginia. The objectives were to (i) determine the initial form and fate of P and K during mine soil weathering, (ii) predict the long-term behavior and P and K supplying potential of spoils when used as topsoil substitutes, and (iii) recommend corrective measures to optimize mine spoil revegetation strategies with regard to P and K fertility. Study materials, methods and results are discussed.

entry.dc:title: DESIGN AND PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS IN SURFACE-MINED LAND SHAPING.
entry.dc:creator: Harwood G.
entry.dc:description: In the context of surface mine spoil regrading, this paper reviews mining literature within the scope of: grading operations, planning, spoil pile design, recontouring and sediment pond design, grading equipment design and operation, costs, computer programs related to questions of design and operation, etc. The literature search included several electronic databases and other more traditional sources.

entry.dc:title: Use of Bucket Wheel Excavators Under Severe Conditions.
entry.dc:creator: Vogt W.
entry.dc:description: The surface coal mines at Neyveli (India) and Goonyella (Queensland) use bucket wheel excavators to work solidified and abrasive material. The use of bucket wheel excavators in surface of Bukit Asam (Sumatra) is also characterized by high cutting force requirements. In addition, the area is known for its high precipitation. In the lignite surface mine of Elbistan (Turkey) intermediate hard rock layers hinder overburden stripping. Using the above-mentioned projects as examples, the operating problems of bucket wheel excavators under severe conditions are discussed, and solutions to these problems are indicated. Finally, the technical and operational preconditions for successful use of bucket wheel excavators under extreme winter conditions are cited.

entry.dc:title: Tall fescue production and nutrient status on southwest Virginia mine soils
entry.dc:creator: Roberts J.
entry.dc:description: Tall fescue (Festuca arundinacea Schreb.) is a hardy grass species commonly used in surface mine reclamation and soil conservation. This study documented changes in fescue production (five growing seasons) and nutrient status (three growing seasons) as influenced by spoil type and various amendments. In Exp. I, fescue growth and nutrient status on five mixes of fertilized sandstone (SS) and siltstone (SiS) spoils were compared. A 2:1 SS/SiS control and treatments of 112 Mg ha<sup>-1</sup> sawdust, native topsoil, and 22, 56, 112, and 224 Mg ha<sup>-1</sup> municipal sewage sludge were compared in Exp. II. Standing biomass was measured in 1982-1984 and 1986 and tissue nutrient levels were measured in 1982-1984. High SiS spoils inhibited initial biomass production in Exp. I, but parent material effects diminished with time. All spoil mixes maintained adequate fescue production for five growing seasons, primarily due to small annual N additions (56 kg ha<sup>-1</sup>). In Exp. II, highest yields were maintained on ≥ 56 Mg ha<sup>-1</sup> sludge treatments. Fescue production declined consistently through 1984 in all other treatments, probably due to N stress. Fescue production was highest the second year (1983) in all treatments of both experiments, but dropped sharply in 1984. Overall results indicate N was most limiting to production in the short term, but P becomes limiting over time. Sludge-amended soils supported higher N, P, and cation tissue concentrations. Total P uptake appeared to be limited by low N levels, even when adequate soil P was available, potassium uptake rates greatly exceeded K fertilizer applications. Heavy metal uptake was not a problem, even in very high sludge treatments. Sludge-amended mine soils were superior to both native topsoil and inorganically fertilized spoils in their ability to sustain long-term fescue production without periodic augmentation.

entry.dc:title: KENTUCKY MINE FINDS REWARDS IN CAST BLASTING.
entry.dc:creator: Merritt P.
entry.dc:description: Bringing in an 18-cu-yd dragline, maintaining a fleet of 85-ton trucks, and introducing cast blasting have combined to make the Straight Creek surface mine one of eastern Kentucky's competitive steam coal producers. Removal of the 90-ft-thick interburden between seams Nos. 9 and 10 is the task of the dragline and cast blasting. The interburden is drilled and shot in such a manner as to throw a measurable 40% of this material into the adjacent mined-out area.

entry.dc:title: Early seral trends in plant community diversity on a recontoured surface mine
entry.dc:creator: Hatton T.J.
entry.dc:description: The initial floristic composition and structure of vegetation on a recontoured surface mine in southwestern Wyoming was experimentally manipulated to test ideas concerning successional convergence. Experimental treatments involving the planting pattern and density of shrubs and the storage of topsoil were evaluated on the basis of their ability to divert the successional trajectories of the redeveloping vegetation and to increase species diversity. The change in compositional similarity along a topographic gradient was also monitored. The influence of initial composition and soil storage generally declined with time; successional convergence among treatments over the four years of the study was largely monotonic. The planting of shrubs and the storage of topsoil did, however, influence the rate of plant succession. There were no persistent differences in alpha diversity among the experimental treatments. Compositional dissimilarity along the topographic gradient, as expressed by beta diversity, increased with time. © 1987 Dr W. Junk Publishers.

entry.dc:title: Intersection graphic method - a method for calculating quantity of coal and rock by using a computer for selection of surface mining schemes
entry.dc:creator: Tian H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Meitan Xuebao Journal of the China Coal Society
entry.dc:description: This paper proposes a method based on the exhaustion method for calculating the quantity of coal and rock by using a computer for selecting an optimal surface mining scheme provides a mathematical model for the calculations. The system adopts the template technique for producing frustum files. This system has improved the accuracy of calculation by separating different zone so that a variable slope can be varied at different azimuths and depths within the boundary of a surface mine.

entry.dc:title: AMAX TAKES ITS DELTA SURFACE MINE UNDERGROUND.
entry.dc:creator: Trewhitt J.
entry.dc:description: Amax Coal Co. has brought longer life to a former section of its Delta surface mine near Harrisburg, Ill. , by punching entries into the highwall to form a 500,000-tpy underground mine. Delta's mined-out Harco section has been transformed into the company's first highwall mine. If the mine succeeds, the company might create other underground mines when surface operations reach their economic limits. At Harco, surface mining stopped when the overburden to coal ratio reached 24. 27:1.

entry.dc:title: OPEN-PIT PRODUCTION SCHEDULER: ALGORITHM AND IMPLEMENTATION.
entry.dc:creator: Gershon M.
entry.dc:description: An approach for scheduling the mining of ore and waste blocks in a surface mine is presented. While mathematical programming approaches have been developed to solve this problem optimally, they are difficult to implement and understand. The more simplistic approach presented achieves practical mining schedules, taking into account both long- and short-term considerations. The key to the approach is use of the concept of ranked positional grade. The program can determine a complete schedule for a specified time period, or it can be used interactively as a guiding tool for the engineer.

entry.dc:title: COMPUTER PROGRAM MATCHES TRUCKS WITH SHOVELS.
entry.dc:creator: Fytas K.
entry.dc:description: Loading and hauling excavated materials represent a significant component of the total operating cost of a surface mine. Often, costs of a shovel/truck operation can be reduced by applying one of the programs available from equipment dealers and other sources. One program called VEHSIM can calculate truck haul-and-return cycle times and examine the effect of rolling resistance on the productivity of the system. Another program recently developed in Canada, can handle more complex truck/shovel operations by simulating any number of shovels or other types of cyclic loading machines and trucks working together. Called PITSIM II, the program also provides solutions to the problem of optimizing the operation of trucks and shovels of a mixed-size truck fleet.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING OF OIL SANDS IN CANADA: DEVELOPMENTS IN PRODUCTIVITY IMPROVEMENT.
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.K.
entry.dc:description: A variety of equipment is used to surface mine oil sands, including bucket wheel excavators/conveyors, draglines, hydraulic shovels, and off-highway trucks. This paper examines the existing mining schemes and equipment used. Several proposals to improve mine productivity are presented.

entry.dc:title: DRILLING RESEARCH APPLICATIONS TO BLAST DESIGN.
entry.dc:creator: Scoble M.
entry.dc:description: This paper reviews the evolution of drill monitoring research and reports on blasthole drilling investigations in the Montreal area. These studies were aimed at evaluating the contributions of drill performance monitoring to improving various procedures in surface mine design. These include estimation of rock strength and fracturation for optimizing fragmentation; monitoring of drill, rod and bit performance; hole depth and pit floor control; additional provision of geological and mineralization data. The drill monitoring instrumentation used in these studies was a compact, durable and powerful microprocessor-based data acquisition system. This device has the capability of accurately scanning and recording drilling parameters over borehole depth intervals of less than 0. 5 cm.

entry.dc:title: Design, construction and maintenance of surface mine haulage roads
entry.dc:creator: Collins J.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Often laborious evaluations are carried out to select mining equipment with little attention being paid to the design, construction and maintenance of the surface on which this equipment must travel. This paper deals with the many facets of designing surface mine haulage roads identifying elements which are critical to realizing the full potential and productivity of the equipment. More specifically, the influence of grade and rolling resistances on truck productivity has been emphasized. Procedures for properly constructing and maintaining haulage roads have been summarized. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Role of the computer in managing and applying geotechnical data to surface mine design
entry.dc:creator: Wade N.H.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: In large open cast operations, effective management of considerable volumes of specialized data generated by various earth science disciplines is necessary to ensure optimum pit design and equipment utilization. The development of a computerized geotechnical data base for a coal strip mine is described and the interrelationship between the data base and the geological computer model is discussed, highlighting the advantages as well as shortcomings of the systems approach. Geotechnical input to mine development is outlined including computer models for determining safe pitwall and spoilpile slopes, classifying the mine area into sub-areas of relatively consistent geotechnical characteristics and assessing formation diggability. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: A technique for ground characterization using automated production drill monitoring
entry.dc:creator: Scoble M.J.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: The monitoring and interpretation of production drill performance data enables a determination of rock mass strength and structure. Correlation of drill performance parameters with changes in intact rock strength, lithology and frequency of fractures has been shown to provide a means of accurately profiling variation in these rock properties with depth. Case studies undertaken in surface operations, using both analog and digital drill monitoring instrumentation, illustrate the potential of this technique for rock mass characterization in surface mine environments. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: COLONIZATION OF WESTERN WHEATGRASS (AGROPYRON SMITHII RYDB.) BY VESICULAR‐ARBUSCULAR MYCORRHIZAL FUNGI DURING THE REVEGETATION OF A SURFACE MINE
entry.dc:creator: LOREE M.
entry.dc:description: Development of vesicular‐arbuscular mycorrhizas and proliferation of roots of western wheat‐grass (Agropyron smithii Rydb.) were investigated in a revegetated mine soil in southeastern Wyoming, USA. Total rooting density (root length per volume of soil) and spore frequency increased as a function of age of the reclamation (time elapsed since reseeding). Topsoil replaced during reclamation was apparently the primary source of mycorrhizal inoculum in the most recently reclaimed site. Seedlings growing on spoil material without topsoil were generally non‐mycorrhizal, but mycorrhizal rooting density was not significantly correlated with the residual content of soil organic matter (an indicator of the proportion of topsoil in the growth media). Mycorrhizal colonization in sites up to three years old was minimal in spite of rapid increases in overall rooting density. Mean rooting density, mean degree of infection, and mean spore frequencies in older sites (five to seven years) were comparable to those of an adjacent undisturbed rangeland, but were highly variable. Mature, non‐mycorrhizal specimens were observed, suggesting that A. smithii is not highly dependent on mycorrhizal infection for survival on this disturbed site. Copyright © 1987, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Future concepts in surface mining operations.
entry.dc:creator: Atkinson T.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
entry.dc:description: Reviews the current state of conventional equipment; the move to continuous systems (continuous excavators, in-pit crushing, run of mine rock conveying, high-angle conveyors); developments and trends in mine trucks ('trolley assist' truck haulage, mammoth trucks); blasthole drilling; explosives; electrical power systems; electronics; image analysis; ultrasonics; lasers; radio waves; computer technology (artificial intelligence, surface mine design and operational planning). There is a concluding discussion drawn from the meeting at which the paper was presented.-after Authors

entry.dc:title: FECAL COLIFORM CONCENTRATIONS IN RUNOFF FROM A GRAZED, RECLAIMED SURFACE MINE
entry.dc:creator: Boyer D.G.
entry.prism:publicationName: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
entry.dc:description: The relatively scarcity of flat or moderately sloping land in Central Appalachia make reclaimed surface mined lands attractive for agricultural uses. A reclaimed surface coal mine in southern West Virginia was placed under grazing management during the 1984 and 1985 growing seasons. Discharge was collected from summer‐grazed watersheds of about 2.8 ha and 8.9 ha and analyzed, by the membrane‐filtration method, for fecal coliforms (FC). Prior to grazing, in 1984, FC counts were < 20/100 ml. During the grazing season, FC ranged from <0/100 ml to> 1000/100 ml in 1984 and from 0/100 ml to > 2500/100 ml in 1985. FC counts remained high during warm periods for several months after grazing ceased. It was concluded that the bacteriological quality of receiving streams was impacted by grazing the reclaimed area and recommended standards for point sources were often exceeded; however, the FC counts did not appear to be any greater than what would have been expected from grazed, undisturbed areas. Reclaimed surface mine areas in Appalachia have the potential to be a valuable “flat land” resource and grazing appears to be an alternative post mine land use that affects bacteriological water quality in a similar manner as “natural” pastures. However, good management practices may be necessary to avoid bacterial contamination of adjacent bodies of water. Copyright © 1987, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved
